explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the sentence-final punctuation that terminates titles, headings, or boilerplate opening lines—i.e. the period marking the end of a headline or introductory phrase.

This neuron is basically a detector for tiny, high-frequency BPE fragments—mostly closed-class function words or bound morphemes (e.g. “of,” “the,” “its,” “your,” plus short pieces like “st,” “te”). It lights up whenever the model sees these common little tokens.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the final punctuation of short, title- or headline-style lines—i.e. it marks the period (or similar delimiter) that ends a heading or title segment rather than ordinary sentence text.

This neuron lights up whenever the model hits a “linking” word that kicks off a subordinate or adjunct phrase—prepositions (in, on, during, with, beyond, outside, into, of …), subordinating conjunctions (if), participial heads (having/getting), even title‐style connectors. In other words, it marks the start of a PP/SBAR-type unit or modifier clause.
This feature acts as a named‐entity detector, firing strongly on capitalized proper nouns—especially organizations, brands, sports teams and geographic/place names—in news‐style text.

This neuron fires on “identifier” tokens in formal reference contexts—e.g. the page-number in a legal citation (the 3-digit locator after “Cal. App. 2d”), year or volume numbers, and similarly on fully capitalized or uncommon proper names/hashtags (e.g. Bhatadze, Ulloa, GodIsNotGreat). It essentially flags the parts of text that uniquely identify a case, person, tag or record.
This neuron fires on the little “end‐chunks” of library, package or brand names embedded in code (the distinctive trailing n-grams in import paths, URLs, identifiers, header guards, etc.).

This neuron flags high-strength, evaluative “degree” words—those hedges or intensifiers (almost, seemingly, practically, absolutely, good, bad, idealistic, mind-boggling, etc.) that amplify or qualify a statement.
This neuron is simply picking up the subword “it” (the two‐letter sequence i-t) wherever it appears, whether inside English, French, German, or other words.

This neuron fires on the “label” tokens that kick off structured documents—titles, headings or metadata markers—across domains (medical-article and taxon names, blog-post titles, XML tags and attributes like id/AssemblyName, legal-case headings and docket numbers, file names, section IDs, etc.). In effect it detects the special tokens that serve as document or section identifiers.
